transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start off, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well… it’s a bit hard to explain without sounding silly, but I suppose what finally made me think I should talk to someone is that I keep finding myself getting up when I really shouldn’t need to.

Like in staff meetings at school, everyone else will be sitting there, going through the agenda, and I’ll suddenly feel like I need to refill my coffee, or go check a handout at the back of the room, or move over to look at something—when honestly, if I’m being truthful, none of it is urgent. It’s not as if the meeting depends on me doing it right that second. I just get this feeling that I have to be up and moving.

And it happens outside of work too, like at dinner with other people. Everyone’s seated, eating, talking, and I’ll pop up to get water, or adjust something, or clear a plate before anyone’s finished. I don’t always notice I’m doing it until I’m already standing. It’s been embarrassing, really, because I’m 60, I’m a teacher, I should be able to sit through a meeting or a meal like everyone else. But lately it’s been noticeable enough that I thought… all right, maybe I should ask about it.
When you feel the need to get up and move, do you notice any uncomfortable or unpleasant sensation in your legs beforehand that gets better once you start moving?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean, I don’t usually notice a feeling in my legs first, like an ache or a crawling sensation or anything that makes me think, “Oh, my legs are uncomfortable, I need to move them.”

It’s more like… I’m just suddenly up, or I’ve decided I need to do something across the room. Sometimes there’s a sort of internal restlessness, I suppose, but I wouldn’t say it’s specifically in my legs, and I don’t think moving makes a physical sensation go away. It’s not like relief from pain or discomfort. It’s more that sitting still starts to feel impossible, or I get this urge to be doing something.
Are you currently taking, or have you recently started, any new medications—particularly antipsychotics, anti-nausea drugs, or antidepressants?

I don’t think so, no. I’m trying to think through what I take, because I know medication lists can get muddled, but I haven’t recently started anything like that—at least not that I’m aware of.

No antipsychotic medicines, and I don’t think I’ve been given anything for nausea recently. Antidepressants… no, not newly started. I mean, if there’s a particular medication name you’re wondering about, you may have to jog my memory, but nothing comes to mind as new or changed around the time this has been going on.

Thinking back to when you were a child or teenager, did you have similar trouble sitting still, staying in your seat, or feeling restless, or is this something that's really only become noticeable more recently?

Oh, no, it definitely isn’t brand new. I mean, it’s become more embarrassing recently because I’m older and I’m in these professional situations where I really ought to look composed, but if I’m honest, there are little threads of it going right back to childhood.

I remember my school reports saying things like, “bright girl,” or “very capable,” but then there’d always be the bit about not staying in my seat, or needing reminders to wait my turn. And my mother used to joke—half affectionately, half exasperated—that before I was even ten I’d practically worn a path in the classroom floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener. Apparently I was always finding some reason to get up.

At the time I think people just treated it as me being lively or fidgety, not anything serious. But yes, looking back, the sitting still and waiting my turn part was there when I was a child too.
Aside from the restlessness, do you find yourself excessively worrying about a lot of different things—like work, health, or family—more days than not, and having trouble controlling that worry?

I’m not sure I’d say that, no. I mean, I worry about things in the ordinary way—if there’s something going on at work, or if someone in the family has an issue, of course I’ll think about it. But I don’t think I’m spending most days worrying across lots of different areas in a way I can’t control.

It’s more that I can get wound up in the moment, if that makes sense, but I wouldn’t describe myself as constantly anxious about work, health, family, money, all of it. I don’t think worry is the main thing driving the restlessness. At least, it doesn’t feel that way to me.
